newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BRIBES SCANDALS RAISE TENSION IN BELGIAN COALITION.
newsitem.headline: BRIBES SCANDALS RAISE TENSION IN BELGIAN COALITION.

text.p: Tension crept through the Belgian government over the weekend as three partners in the centre-left coalition tried to work out how to deal with bribery allegations surrounding the fourth.

The PS party of French-speaking socialists is at the heart of a controversy over illegal party financing after recent allegations that it received millions of francs in return for favours to companies.
Monday sees the weekly meetings of managers of government and opposition parties and there can be no doubt the PS scandals are high on the agendas.
So far after last week's disclosures all sides have been remarkably reticent about any implications for the coalition.

But as public opinion increasingly wonders how many PS officials will be linked to the bribes-for-orders scandals and how often police will have to raid the party's headquarters in the search for evidence, calls for action are not far away.

Crucially, PS leaders will wonder how the CVP party of Flemish christian-democrats -- the largest coalition partner -- will take news of Luxembourg bank accounts held by senior PS officials who are struggling to explain the origin of millions of francs in the accounts.

When the so-called Dassault scandal resurfaced last month after lying dormant for months as police arrested and charged two senior PS aides, the CVP did not hesitate to bear down on the PS with a demand the party get its house in order soon.
Cracks appeared in the coalition as CVP Youth members called for a cabinet reshuffle and a liberal opposition party offered to take the PS's place in the government.
PS leaders called for all those who had committed "faults" to come clean. But they also defended themselves by denying any involvement with shady practices dating back to a previous generation.
Belgium did not restrict corporate funding of political parties until 1989 and only banned it completely in 1993.

By putting pressure on the PS, the CVP managed to bring about the resignation of the PS's previous chairman Guy Spitaels from senior posts in the legislature of Wallonia, Belgium's francophone southern half.
But the recent fresh revelations mean the party's credibility as a coalition partner is still in question
On Friday current PS chairman Philippe Busquin acknowledged for the first time the party had had contacts with two firms at the centre of the allegations about illegal party financing.
The Dassault and Agusta scandals centre on claims the French and Italian companies of the same names bribed Belgian parties in the late 1980s to win lucrative defence contracts.
Both firms have denied any wrongdoing.

Busquin, who took over in 1992, said he was unaware of any illegal payments. But after a police search of the party's headquarters on Thursday, he said he had learned the party received 1.2 million francs from Dassault in 1987.
Busquin also acknowledged meeting Agusta representatives in 1988 before the company won a contract to supply the army with 46 helicopters, a deal also being scrutinised by police.

Present PS leaders have been under pressure to clarify what they know since the arrest last month of two party officials, said by their lawyers to have accepted 30 million Belgian francs (about $1 million) from Dassault, rekindled the bribes probes.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene has so far held the coalition together in the face of opposition calls for the PS to pull out. Last week the government easily defeated motions of no confidence brought against it in Parliament.
Dehaene, keen to finish preparations for Belgium's entry into Europe's economic and monetary union, has said the scandals are an internal problem for the PS.
